{{Short description|Ancient hill-top citadel in Jerusalem}} {{Infobox historic site | name = Antonia Fortress | native_names = {{native name|he|מבצר אנטוניה}}
{{native name|arc|קצטרא דאנטוניה}} | image = File:The Antonia Fortress.jpg | alt = | caption = Proposed reconstruction of the Antonia Fortress at the [[Holyland Model of Jerusalem]] | pushpin_map = | pushpin_alt = | location = [[Jerusalem during the Second Temple period|Jerusalem]] | coordinates = {{Coord|31|46|48|N|35|14|01|E|type:landmark_scale:5000|display=inline}} | type = [[fortress]] | builder = [[Herod the Great|Herod]] | material = | built = First century BC | abandoned = First century AD | epochs = [[Judaea|early Roman period]] | excavations = | archaeologists = | condition = | public_access = Limited }}The '''Antonia Fortress''' ([[Aramaic]]: קצטרא דאנטוניה){{efn|Based on Josephus' use of the word 'citadel' or 'fortress' when referring to the Antonia Fortress}} was a [[citadel]] built by [[Herod the Great]] and named for Herod's patron [[Mark Antony]], as a fortress whose chief function was to protect the [[Second Temple]]. It was built in [[Jerusalem]] at the eastern end of the Second Wall, at the north-western corner of the [[Temple Mount]], and was connected to the Temple by [[Portico|porticoes]]. ==History== === Construction === The Antonia Fortress was built by [[Herod the Great]] (r. 37–4 BC), the [[Client kingdoms in ancient Rome|client king]] of [[Herodian kingdom|Judaea]], who named it after his then-patron, the Roman politician and general [[Mark Antony]]. The fort replaced the [[Hasmonean Judea|Hasmonean]] fortress known as the [[Hasmonean Baris|Baris]], which had occupied the site, and possibly an [[Ptolemaic Baris|earlier fortress]] or fortresses built by the [[Ptolemaic Kingdom|Ptolemies]] and/or [[Seleucid Empire|Seleucids]].{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=134}} It remains unclear whether the Baris was entirely demolished, only partly dismantled, or retained and enlarged when the Antonia was built.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=135}} Netzer assumes that the entire Baris was demolished, although he acknowledges that this is uncertain.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=134}} Bahat, by contrast, suggests that only its southern part was destroyed, with the northern part preserved and incorporated into the new structure.{{sfn|Bahat|2015|p=17}} ==== Date ==== Ehud Netzer dated the construction of the Antonia Fortress to around 35 BC and proposed that it was adapted to the enlarged [[Temple Mount]] around 20 BC.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=138}}[[File:P8170045.JPG|right|thumb|254x254px|A model of the Antonia Fortress—currently in the [[Israel Museum]]]]The exact construction date is disputed because the fortress's name suggests that Herod built it before Mark Antony's defeat at [[Battle of Actium|Actium]] by [[Augustus|Octavian]] in 31 BC and Antony's suicide in 30 BC. Herod was known as an astute diplomat and pragmatist who consistently aligned himself with Rome's winning side and its dominant political figure. This proposed date is also difficult to reconcile with the presumed date of construction of the [[Herodian Temple]]. === First Jewish Revolt === The fortress was one of the last strongholds of the [[Jews]] in the [[Siege of Jerusalem (70 AD)]], when the Second Temple was destroyed.{{cite book |title=Jerusalem, Israel, Petra & Sinai |publisher=[[DK (publisher)|DK]] |isbn=978-1-4654-4131-7 |year=2016 |orig-year=2000 |page=48}} Netzer proposed that the Antonia hill was levelled at some point during the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyad]] period, in connection with work on the Temple Mount.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|pp=135, 138}} == Location == The Antonia Fortress stood at the northwest corner of the Temple Mount.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=134}} The first-century historian [[Josephus]] described the site as follows: {{Blockquote|text=Now as to the tower of Antonia, it was situated at the corner of two cloisters of the court of the [[Second Temple|temple]]; of that on the west, and that on the north; it was erected upon a rock of fifty cubits in height, and was on a great precipice.|author=Josephus|title=[[The Jewish War]]|source=5.238 (translation by [[William Whiston]])}} [[File:PikiWiki_Israel_68677_fortress_of_antonia.jpg|thumb|A 19th-century photograph of a rock scarp north of the Temple Mount, hewn beneath [[Mamluk Sultanate|Mamluk]]-era structures, believed to have been cut by Herod during the construction of the Antonia Fortress]] The fortress's boundaries to the west, north, and east are only partly known archaeologically, so its exact extent on those sides cannot be fully reconstructed, though the surviving evidence allows some general conclusions.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=135}} On the north, a [[moat]] is thought to have separated the Antonia from the area now occupied by Jerusalem's [[Muslim Quarter (Jerusalem)|Muslim Quarter]], extending to some degree along the west and east sides as well.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=135}} The southern side is better attested through a vertical rock-cut scarp, about 93 metres long and up to 12 metres high, which marks the edge of the hill.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=135}} A channel cut nearby carried water to the site; its northern section is generally attributed to the Hasmonean period.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=135}} == Description == {{Blockquote|text=In the first place, the rock itself was covered over with smooth pieces of stone, from its foundation, both for ornament, and that anyone who would either try to get up or to go down it might not be able to hold his feet upon it. Next to this, and before you come to the edifice of the tower itself, there was a wall three cubits high; but within that wall all the space of the tower of Antonia itself was built upon, to the height of forty cubits. The inward parts had the largeness and form of a palace, it being parted into all kinds of rooms and other conveniences, such as courts, and places for bathing, and broad spaces for camps; insomuch that, by having all conveniences that cities wanted, it might seem to be composed of several cities, but by its magnificence it seemed a palace. And as the entire structure resembled that of a tower, it contained also four other distinct towers at its four corners; whereof the others were but fifty cubits high; whereas that which lay upon the southeast corner was seventy cubits high, that from thence the whole temple might be viewed; but on the corner where it joined to the two cloisters of the temple, it had passages down to them both, through which the guard (for there always lay in this tower a Roman legion) went several ways among the cloisters, with their arms, on the Jewish festivals, in order to watch the people, that they might not there attempt to make any innovations. for the temple was a fortress that guarded the city, as was the tower of Antonia a guard to the temple; and in that tower were the guards of those three.|author=Josephus|title=The Jewish War|source=5.239–245 (translation by William Whiston)}} === Netzer's proposed reconstruction === [[Ehud Netzer]], an archaeologist and leading authority on [[Herodian architecture]], noted a resemblance between Josephus's description of the Antonia and [[Herodium]], the hilltop palace-fortress he himself excavated. Both were built by Herod and combined a main structure with projecting towers, although the central structure was circular at [[Herodium]] and square or nearly square at the Antonia.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=134}} Netzer proposed a reconstruction of the Antonia as an 86-by-86-metre near-square structure, about 18 metres high, with a tower at each corner projecting only slightly beyond the footprint. Three of the towers, each about 19 by 19 metres and 23 metres high, were modelled on Herodium's eastern tower and the [[Tower of David (northeast tower)|Phasael]], Hippicus, and Mariamne towers in Jerusalem's eastern wall. The fourth, at the Antonia's southeastern corner, was reconstructed as the tallest and largest, about 22 by 22 metres and 28 metres high. A 1.5-metre-high wall topped with [[Merlon|merlons]] was reconstructed around the central building, set back to leave a passage of similar width.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=138}}[[File:Holy_Land_2018_(2)_P071_Jerusalem_Convent_of_the_Sisters_of_Zion_Museum.jpg|thumb|A capital and base likely from the Antonia Fortress, now displayed in the [[Convent of the Sisters of Zion]]]] Netzer's reconstruction divides the central building into two wings, each enclosing a courtyard of about 18 by 42 metres ringed by two-storey [[Stoa|stoas]] (porticoes). Their upper storey gave access to the rooms on that level.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=138}} Two smaller inner courtyards lay between the wings, also surrounded by porticoes, which Netzer suggests served mainly to light and ventilate the building and to connect its various parts.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=138}} The royal wing housed a bathhouse and a reception hall comparable in plan to the two large [[triclinium]] halls excavated at [[Hasmonean and Herodian royal winter palaces|Herod's winter palace]] in [[Jericho]]. While most of the building rose two storeys, the triclinium hall was full-height, its surrounding third storey formed by a single row of rooms on each side.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=138}} Netzer further reconstructs a narrow passage, about 1.5 metres wide, separating the central building from its surrounding wall for guards patrolling the fortress's perimeter.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=141}} Guard posts are likewise proposed at the corners and entrances of the four towers, in addition to the external staircases. Netzer proposes that flights of steps were added once the Temple Mount was later enlarged.{{sfn|Netzer|2007|p=141}} ==Christian tradition== Traditionally, [[Christians]] have believed for centuries that the vicinity of the Antonia Fortress was the site of [[Pontius Pilate]]' ''[[praetorium]]'', where [[Jesus]] was [[Pilate's court|tried]] for [[high treason]]. This was based on the assumption that an area of Roman flagstones discovered beneath the [[Church of the Condemnation]] and the [[Convent of the Sisters of Zion]] was '[[Gabbatha|the pavement]]' which {{bibleverse||John|19:13|}} describes as the location of Jesus' trial. ===Antonia pavement: archaeological counter-arguments=== [[Pierre Benoit (archaeologist)|Pierre Benoit]], former professor of New Testament studies at the [[École Biblique]], reexamined the results of all previous surveys of the north-western escarpment of the Haram, of the archaeological studies of the sites owned by the Catholics in the area (Convent of the Sisters of Zion, [[Church of the Flagellation|Flagellation Monastery]] and [[Church of Saint Anne, Jerusalem|St Anne Convent]] of the [[White Fathers]]), as well as the digs north of the [[Struthion Pool]] area, and published in 1971 his conclusions: Archaeological investigation indicates that about a century after the presumed time of Jesus' death, this area was rebuilt as the eastern of two [[Roman Forum|forums]] belonging to the new city initiated by [[Hadrian]] in around 130 AD, the [[Aelia Capitolina]],{{cite journal |last= Benoit |first= Pierre |author-link= Pierre Benoit (archaeologist) |title= L'Antonia d'Hérode le Grand et le forum oriental d'Aelia Capitolina |journal=[[Harvard Theological Review]] |publisher= Cambridge University Press |location= Cambridge, U.K. |volume= 64 |issue= 2–3 |pages= 135–167 [155–156, 159–161] |year= 1971 |doi= 10.1017/S0017816000032478 |jstor= 1509294 |s2cid= 162902370 |issn= 0017-8160 |language= fr |url= http://www.jstor.org/stable/1509294 |access-date= 8 September 2020 |url-access= subscription }} and it is conceivable that following the destruction of the Antonia Fortress during the siege of 70 AD, its pavement tiles were reused at Hadrian's forum.{{cite web|url=http://www.jerusalemexperience.com/tour/ecce-homo-arch-notre-dame-de-sion-convent-via-dolorosa/|title=Ecce Homo Arch Video|website=Jerusalem Experience|year=2012}} However, he also considers the possibility that the pavement is from Hadrian's time altogether. The eastern forum of the Aelia Capitolina was built over the Struthion Pool, which was mentioned by Josephus as being adjacent to the fortress (Josephus, ''Jewish War'' 5:11:4).{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} ===Praetorium at royal palace, not at Antonia=== There are textual and archaeological arguments against the [[Pilate's court|trial of Jesus]] being carried out at the Antonia Fortress. Like [[Philo]], Josephus testifies that the Roman governors stayed in [[Herod's Palace (Jerusalem)|Herod's Palace]] while they were in Jerusalem,Benoit (1976), p. 87 and carried out their trials on the pavement immediately outside it (Josephus, ''The Jewish War'', 2:14:8). Josephus indicates that Herod's Palace is on the Western Hill (''The'' ''Jewish War'', 5:2) and in 2001 some of its vestiges were rediscovered under a corner of the [[Tower of David]].Jacqueline Schaalje, "Israeli Archaeologists Discover Herod's Palace", The Jewish Magazine (October 2001). Archaeologists therefore conclude that in the first century, the ''praetorium''—the residence of the ''[[praefectus]]'' (governor)—was in the former royal palace on the Western Hill, rather than at the Antonia Fortress, on the opposite side of the city. However, as the tradition retained its power in associating the fortress with Jesus' trial, the place where it once stood serves as the starting point of the ''[[Via Dolorosa]]'' commemorating the [[crucifixion of Jesus]]. ===Two arguments for Antonia as the place of judgement=== 1. During the greatest pilgrimage feast, when hundreds of thousands came to the Temple, Pilate likely had to be with his garrison next to the Temple mount as a potential focus of the uprising, and certainly the favorite place of religious and national zealots who wished independence from Rome.{{cite web|url=https://dannythedigger.com/via-dolorosa/|title=The Via Dolorosa|website=Danny the Digger|year=2023}} 2. According to Luke's Gospel ({{bibleverse-nb|Luke|23:6{{ndash}}13|ASV}}), Pilate found out that Christ was from Galilee, "and when he knew that he was of Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him unto Herod, who himself also was at Jerusalem in these days" (23:7). Herod Antipas, who came for the holiday from Galilee to Jerusalem, disappointed and angry because of Jesus’ silence, "sent him back to Pilate" (23:11), who then "called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people" (23:13). It seems that Pilate was not in Herod's castle. If the trial had taken place in Herod's castle, he could have simply asked Herod to come to the courtroom, as he summoned the chief priests and the leaders.{{cite web|url=https://www.holylandsite.com/via-dolorosa/|title=The Via Dolorosa|website=Holy Land Site|year=2023}} ==Other theories== Some researchers and academics, including Marilyn Sams (M.A. in American Literature, Brigham Young University) and [[Robert Cornuke]] (Ph.D. in Bible and Theology, Louisiana Baptist University), have expanded on research by [[Ernest L. Martin]] (1932–2002, meteorologist, college professor, amateur archeologist), who offered evidence that the compound on what is commonly called the Temple Mount did not house the Jerusalem Temple, but is instead the remnants of a more massive Antonia Fortress, and that the rock inside the [[Dome of the Rock]] is not the [[Foundation Stone]], but was inside the [[Praetorium]] of [[Pontius Pilate]] where Jesus was judged.{{cite journal |last= Sams |first= Marilyn |title= A Proposal for the Configuration of Solomon's Temple Mount |website= academia.edu |url= https://www.academia.edu/35235638 |access-date= 9 December 2020}} [[Jerome Murphy-O'Connor]], however, argued that this theory "cannot be sustained", as it cannot be reconciled with Josephus' description, and it "does not account for the archaeological remains in the western section of the north wall".{{cite journal |last= Murphy-O'Connor |first= Jerome |author-link= Jerome Murphy-O'Connor |title= Where was the Antonia Fortress? |journal= Revue Biblique |pages= 78–89 |publisher=[[École Biblique]] |location= Jerusalem |volume= 111 |number= 1 |year= 2004 |jstor= 44824413 |url= https://www.jstor.org/stable/44824413 |access-date= 9 December 2020}} Josephus and archaeology don't leave much space for doubt in regard to the fact that the Temple Mount was indeed the site of the Herodian Temple, nor for the location of the Antonia near its north-western corner.[[File:P8170052.JPG|right|thumb|250px|Model of the fortress and the Tedi Gate (small gate with triangular top)]] Both Josephus and archaeology concur that the Roman military camp after the 70 AD destruction was centered on the [[Tower of David#Herod's towers|three towers]] next to [[Herod's Palace (Jerusalem)|Herod's royal palace]] on the Western Hill, and not on the Temple Mount, whose protective walls had been thrown down by the Romans, with the resulting debris visible until today along the [[Western Wall]] near [[Robinson's Arch]]. Roman military camps had rounded corners and four gates, one in each wall – the Herodian compound had angular corners and nine gates. Permanent camps were much larger, 50 acres on average; the Haram esplanade only contains 36 acres. There is no Roman camp explanation for the Hebrew inscription marking the [[Trumpeting Place inscription|Trumpeting Place]]. The Temple compound was surrounded by porticos (roofed [[colonnade]]s following the inner walls of the compound), while military camps never were. Augustus trusted Herod and would not have built a controlling fortress towering over his capital and Temple, but no emperor would have gone so far as to entrust a legion to a client king. Remains of a 4-metre thick wall and Herodian-style [[ashlar]]s are still observable inside the [[Mamluk Egypt|Mamluk]] buildings in the north-west corner of the Haram and the adjacent area along its northern wall. Together they suggest the dimensions of the Antonia: 112 by 40 metres on the outside, signifying a 3300 square metre floor area, absolutely enough for a small garrison, but certainly not for the entire legion suggested by Martin. Antonia did stand on a rocky outcrop, as written by Josephus, but here, as elsewhere in his writings, he did exaggerate its elevation above the surrounding ground. This still meant that the fortress dominated the Temple courts and porticos, the latter by over ten metres, matching Josephus' words: "the tower of Antonia lay at the angle where the two porticos, the western and the northern, of the first court of the Temple met" ([[The Jewish War|JW]] 5:238), and "[a]t the point where the Antonia impinged on the porticos of the temple there were stairs leading down to both of them by which the guards descended" (JW 5:243; cf. {{bibleverse|Acts|21:40}}). The position and dimensions of those porticos can still be in part discerned, thanks to three surviving roof beam sockets carved out of the living rock of the rocky outcrop which once held the Antonia, north-west of the esplanade. Josephus' statement that all the porticos surrounding the Temple complex measured six stadia "including the Antonia" (JW 5:192) is off by a large margin (six stadia represent about 1.11 km, whereas the sides of the Haram esplanade today measure together about 1.55 km), but it clearly suggests that the fortress was contiguous with the Temple complex with no need for a "double causeway" to connect the two by spanning a distance of one ''[[stade (unit)|stade]]'' (c. 150 m), as claimed by Martin. ==See also== *[[Bezetha]] *[[Convent of the Sisters of Zion|Church of Ecce Homo]] *[[Hasmonean Baris]] *[[Herodian architecture]] ==References== '''Footnotes''' {{Notelist}} '''Citations''' {{Reflist|33em}} == Bibliography == * {{Cite journal |last=Netzer |first=Ehud |author-link=Ehud Netzer |date=2007 |title=The Antonia—Its Initial Location and Form / איפה עמדה האנטוניה ומה הייתה צורתה? |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23630890 |journal=Eretz-Israel: Archaeological, Historical and Geographical Studies / ארץ-ישראל: מחקרים בידיעת הארץ ועתיקותיה |publisher=Israel Exploration Society |language=he |volume=28 |pages=134–143 |issn=0071-108X}} * {{Cite journal |last=Bahat |first=Dan |author-link=Dan Bahat |date=2015 |title="The Fortress Called Baris that Became the Antonia"? / "המצודה שבעבר נקראה באריס ולימים אנטוניה"? |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24433045 |journal=Eretz-Israel: Archaeological, Historical and Geographical Studies / ארץ-ישראל: מחקרים בידיעת הארץ ועתיקותיה |language=he |publisher=Israel Exploration Society |volume=31 |pages=12–19 |issn=0071-108X}} ==External links== *{{Jewish Encyclopedia|article=Antonia|url=http://jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/1614-antonia|author=Lieut.-Col. [[File:Huldah Gates3344.JPG|thumb|Reconstruction of the Herodian Hulda Gates.]]
The '''Huldah Gates''' ({{langx|he|שערי חולדה}}, ''Sha'arei Hulda'') were one of the [[Gates of the Old City of Jerusalem]] leading into the [[Jerusalem Temple]] compound in the [[Hasmonean]] period and were named as such in the [[Mishnah]].<ref name="EJ963"/> The term is currently being used for the remains of two later sets of gates, the Triple Gate and [[the Double Gate]], known together as the Huldah Gates,<ref>{{cite book |last= Gonen |first= Rivka |title= Contested Holiness: Jewish, Muslim, and Christian Perspectives on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem |publisher=[[Ktav Publishing House]] |date=2003 |location= Jersey City, N.J. |page=[https://archive.org/details/contestedholines00rivk/page/32 32] |language=en |oclc= 470185481 |isbn= 9780881257984 |url= https://archive.org/details/contestedholines00rivk |url-access= registration }}</ref> built as part of the much extended [[Herod the Great|Herodian]] [[Temple Mount]], situated in [[Old City (Jerusalem)|Jerusalem's Old City]].<ref name="OConnor"/> Both sets of gates were set into the [[Southern Wall]] of the Temple compound and gave access to the Temple Mount esplanade by means of underground vaulted ramps.<ref name="OConnor"/> Both were walled up in the Middle Ages.<ref name="OConnor">{{cite book |title= The Holy Land: An Oxford Archaeological Guide from Earliest Times to 1700 |series= Oxford Archaeological Guides |author= Jerome Murphy-O'Connor |year= 2008 |location= Oxford |publisher= Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-923666-4 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=m3Yy9FDcT8gC&q=Hulda&pg=PA113 |pages= 104, 113 |access-date=27 July 2019 }}</ref>

The western set is a double-arched gate (the '''Double Gate'''), and the eastern is a triple-arched gate (the '''Triple Gate''').<ref name="OConnor"/> There still are a few Herodian architectural elements visible outside and inside the gates, while most everything else of what we see today is later, Muslim-period work.<ref name="OConnor"/>

==Etymology==
The name "Huldah gates" is taken from the description of the Temple Mount in the [[Mishnah]] (Tractate of [[Middot (Talmud)|Midot]] 1:3).<ref name="EJ963">Encyclopædia Judaica (ed. 1972), vol. 15, pp. 963-4</ref>

Two possible etymologies are given for the name: "Huldah" means "mole" or "mouse" in Hebrew, and the tunnels leading up from these gates called to mind the holes or tunnels used by these animals. Alternatively, in a possible folk etymology, the [[First Temple]] prophetess [[Huldah]]<ref>2 Kgs 22:14-20</ref><ref>Encyclopædia Judaica (ed. 1972), vol. 8, p. 1063</ref> was said to have held court in this area and, indeed, her tomb<ref>Encyclopædia Judaica (ed. 1972), vol. 9, p. 1553 (Tos. Neg. 6:2)</ref> was placed here by some as well.

==Identification==
Accepted opinion amongst scholars is that the Mishna's description (see under [[Huldah Gates#Etymology|Etymology]]) refers to the sanctified area of the Temple Mount in the [[Hasmonean]] period. Therefore, calling the gates found in the current southern wall "Huldah" would be an [[anachronism]], as the base of that wall is part of [[Herod the Great|Herod]]'s post-Hasmonean extension of the Temple Mount.{{citation needed|date=July 2019}}

==Archaeology==
The 19th century excavations of the area by [[Charles Warren]]<ref>Encyclopædia Judaica (ed. 1972), vol. 9, p. 1525</ref> discovered an erratic series of passageways under the triple gate, some leading below the wall and beyond the Mount's southern edge. The purpose and age of these passages are unknown, and more recent archaeologists have not been allowed to investigate due to the political volatility of the site. The passageways from both gates are now used by the [[waqf]] as [[mosque]]s.{{citation needed|date=July 2019}}

==Description==
Both the Double and Triple Gates of the Herodian time allowed access to the Temple Mount esplanade via a vestibule followed by underground vaulted ramps.<ref name="OConnor"/> They have both been blocked since the Middle Ages, and the underground access routes have been partially or fully reconstructed during the Umayyad and later reconstructions and repair work.<ref name="OConnor"/>

===Double Gate===
[[The Double Gate]] was blocked by the construction of a medieval tower in front of it, probably during Fatimid era.<ref name="madaindouble">{{cite web |title=Double Huldah Gate (al-Aqsa al-Qadimi) |url=https://madainproject.com/double_hulda_gate |website=Madain project |access-date=1 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190901151659/https://madainproject.com/double_hulda_gate |archive-date=1 September 2019 |location=WayBack Machine}}</ref><ref name="OConnor"/> Today a small library is established within the remains of this medieval-era fortification tower.<ref name="madaindouble" /> Of what we see today, which is part of the right (eastern) gate, the lintel and the relieving arch above it are Herodian, while the intricately carved cornice is [[Umayyad]].<ref name="OConnor"/> Only the eastern portal of the twin, now blocked, gate is partially visible today.<ref name="madaindouble" />

Inside the Double Gate there is a vestibule with large columns (at least three) supporting two pairs of domes.<ref name="madaindouble" /> The central columns and two more flanking the steps are Herodian, and have recently been reinforced with concrete frames.<ref name="madaindouble" /> The domes though seem to be from an early seventh-century (Early Muslim) reconstruction.<ref name="OConnor"/>

When the [[Al-Aqsa Mosque]] was built, the old steps were blocked, and the eastern aisle lengthened so that new steps from its end would exit north of the mosque, so essentially the exit on the Temple Mount moved eastwards somewhat. The mosque's [[al-Khataniyya Library]] was also established in the remains of the Fatimid-era fortification tower, today entered through the western portal of the twin gate.<ref name="madaindouble" />

===Triple Gate===
The Triple Gate was blocked in the 11th century.<ref name="OConnor"/> The western [[jamb]] is Herodian, while the rest of what we see today is [[Umayyad]].<ref name="OConnor"/>

Inside the Triple Gate, in Herodian times there must have been a passageway identical to the one inside the Double Gate.<ref name="OConnor"/> Its remains now connect to the so-called "[[Solomon's Stables|Al-Marwani Mosque (Solomon's Stables)]]", initially a pillared Herodian substructure of his enlarged Temple esplanade, with some Herodian elements still visible, but repeatedly repaired and rebuilt over the centuries and used since 1996 as a mosque.<ref name="OConnor"/>

The interior of the Triple Gate is similar to that of the Double Gate, though the longer aisle is to the west, and its third aisle, on the east, forms the western boundary of the vaulted area known as ''[[Solomon's Stables|Al-Marwani Mosque (Solomon's Stables)]]''.{{citation needed|date=July 2019}}

{{Short description|Roman period street in Jerusalem}}
[[File:Elef Millim - City of David www.mapah.co.il hirodion up.jpg|thumb|right|The street ascending toward the Temple Mount]]

The '''stepped street''', as it is known from academic works,<ref name=ESI2016>{{cite web |first1= Nahshon |last1= Szanton |first2= Joe |last2= Uziel |title= Jerusalem, City of David [stepped street dig, July 2013 - end 2014], Preliminary Report (21/08/2016) |website=[[Hadashot Arkheologiyot]] |publisher=[[Israel Antiquities Authority]] |volume= 128 |year= 2016 |url= http://www.hadashot-esi.org.il/report_detail_eng.aspx?id=25046&mag_id=124 |access-date= 24 July 2020}}</ref> or the '''Jerusalem pilgrim road''' as it has been dubbed by the [[Ir David Foundation]],<ref>[https://www.cityofdavid.org.il/en/events/pilgrimage-road-revealed-%E2%80%93-live-tour The Pilgrimage Road Revealed], City of David homepage, accessed 24 July 2020</ref> is the [[Judaea (Roman province)|early Roman period]] street connecting the [[Temple Mount]] from its southwestern corner, to [[Jerusalem]]'s southern gates of the time via the [[Pool of Siloam]].<ref name=ESI2016/> The stepped street was built at the earliest during the 30s CE, with the latest coin found under the pavement dating to 30–31 CE, during the governorship of [[Pontius Pilate]]<ref name=ESI2016/> of [[New Testament]] fame. The street is part of the [[City of David (archaeological site)|City of David archaeological park]] located in the [[Jerusalem Walls National Park]] in [[East Jerusalem]].  While the area has been referred to as Mount Ophel<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tribune |first=International Herald |date=2003-12-31 |title=Opinion {{!}} 1928: City of David Uncovered: IN OUR PAGES: 100, 75 AND 50 YEARS AGO |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/31/opinion/IHT-1928-city-of-david-uncovered-in-our-pages-100-75-and-50-years-ago.html |access-date=2026-03-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> or the City of David<ref>{{Cite news |last=Feron |first=James |date=1970-08-02 |title=Walking the Walls Of Old Jerusalem |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/08/02/archives/walking-the-walls-of-old-jerusalem.html |access-date=2026-03-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> by archaeologists and tourists, it is commonly referred to as the [[Wadi Hilweh]] area of [[Silwan]] by local residents.

==Description==
{{See also|Jerusalem Water Channel}}

[[File:City of David - The Stepped Pilgrims Road IMG 5939.JPG|thumb|Idealized representation of the route from the [[Pool of Siloam]] to the [[Temple in Jerusalem|Temple Mount]]]]

The street ascended from Jerusalem's southern gates,<ref name=ESI2016/> along the ancient [[City of David (historic)|City of David]], today part of the [[Palestinians|Palestinian]] neighborhood of [[Silwan]], into what is now the [[Old City (Jerusalem)|Old City]] and passed by the [[Western Wall]]<ref name=Ackerman>{{cite news |author= Ackerman, Gwen |date= 25 January 2011 |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-01-25/archaeologists-discover-ancient-pilgrim-road-through-jerusalem-s-old-city.html |title= Archaeologists Discover Ancient Pilgrim Road Through Jerusalem's Old City |publisher= Bloomberg |access-date=18 January 2014}}</ref> after passing underneath the Herodian bridge now known as [[Robinson's Arch]].<ref name=ESI2016/> The ancient path was improved and paved in large, well-cut stone in the pattern of two steps followed by a long landing, followed by two more steps and another landing. The street was eight meters wide and its length from the Pool of Siloam to the Temple Mount is 600 meters.<ref name=Hasson>{{cite news |date=14 September 2009 |title= Archeologists find main Jerusalem street from Second Temple period |author= Hasson, Nir |url= https://www.haaretz.com/print-edition/news/archeologists-find-main-j-lem-street-from-second-temple-period-1.7951 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110606215015/http://www.haaretz.com/print-edition/news/archeologists-find-main-j-lem-street-from-second-temple-period-1.7951 |url-status= dead |archive-date= June 6, 2011 |newspaper= Haaretz |access-date=18 January 2014}}</ref>

The [[Jerusalem Water Channel|large drainage channel]] which ran below the street<ref name=ESI2016/> has also been excavated and made partially accessible to visitors.

==Archaeological exploration history==
Sections of the ancient street were first discovered by [[Charles Warren]] in 1884,<ref name=ESI2016/> followed by [[Frederick J. Bliss]] and [[Archibald C. Dickey]] of the [[Palestine Exploration Fund]] between 1894 and 1897. The find was reburied when their excavation concluded. Other sections were uncovered, then reburied, by later archaeologists, Jones in 1937 and [[Kathleen Kenyon]] in  1961–1967.<ref>[http://www.gojerusalem.com/article_1176/Second-Temple-Period-Street-Discovered Second Temple Period Street Discovered, at gojerusalem.com] {{webarchive |url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100617084411/http://www.gojerusalem.com/article_1176/Second-Temple-Period-Street-Discovered |date= 17 June 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author= Bedien, David |title= Ancient Temple Street Discovered Beneath Jerusalem |date= 20 September 2009 |newspaper= Philadelphia Bulletin |url= http://thebulletin.us/articles/2009/09/20/news/world/doc4ab6793d7be0b285938366.txt |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160303235027/http://thebulletin.us/articles/2009/09/20/news/world/doc4ab6793d7be0b285938366.txt |url-status= dead |archive-date= 3 March 2016}} <!-- thebulletin.us belongs to a Columbus, GA, newspaper now--></ref> More details about the street were published by [[Benjamin Mazar]] in 1969–1971, followed by [[Ronny Reich]] (alone or in collaboration with Yakov Billig, then [[Eli Shukron]]) between 1999 and 2011 (including findings from the drainage channel running beneath the street), and [[Eilat Mazar]] in 2000.<ref name=ESI2016/>

The street was re-excavated during excavations on a [[Jerusalem Water Channel|water channel]] from the [[Second Temple period]].<ref name=Ackerman/>

== Reception ==
The [[Israel Antiquities Authority]] performed the excavation beneath existing homes using a technique called horizontal excavation.  According to American archaeologist [[Jodi Magness]], “Methodologically, the problem of using a horizontal or tunnel excavation in archaeology is that it doesn’t allow you to see the full context of the remains. Archaeology is all about context, but by digging in this way, you divorce the remains that you excavate from the remains that are above them and around them and that is problematic from an archaeological point of view.”  When asked about the criticism, archaeologist Ari Levy said technology has allowed the archaeologists to overcome many of the obstacles of the excavation, noting that they can't just remove the neighbors’ houses.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Borschel-Dan |first=Amanda |date=17 October 2019 |title=On an ancient road to the Temple, archaeological innovation, mystery and dispute |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/on-an-ancient-road-to-the-temple-archaeological-innovation-mystery-and-dispute/ |access-date=12 October 2024 |work=Times of Israel}}</ref>

The Ir David Foundation, also known as Elad, is a [[Israeli settlement|settler organisation]] that leads excavations in the locale.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2019-06-30 |title=U.S. Envoy Swings Sledgehammer in East Jerusalem, and a Metaphor Is Born (Published 2019) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/30/world/middleeast/ambassador-friedman-jerusalem.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251221095924/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/30/world/middleeast/ambassador-friedman-jerusalem.html |archive-date=2025-12-21 |access-date=2026-03-14 |language=en}}</ref> Archaeologists from the [[Israel Antiquities Authority]] spent twenty years excavating the site.<ref name="Tercatin">{{Cite news |last=Tercatin |first=Rossella |date=2026-02-02 |title=2,000-year-old Pilgrimage Road to Temple Mount opens to public after years of digging |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/2000-year-old-pilgrimage-road-to-temple-mount-opens-to-public-after-years-of-digging/ |access-date=2026-03-14 |work=The Times of Israel |language=en-US |issn=0040-7909}}</ref>  The non-governmental organisation [[Emek Shaveh]] has characterised the archaeological work initiated by Elad an "attempt to redefine the area solely as an ancient site, and not as a Palestinian residential neighborhood".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-10-28 |title=Underground Jerusalem: The excavation of tunnels, channels, and underground spaces in the Historic Basin |url=https://emekshaveh.org/en/underground-jerusalem-the-excavation-of-tunnels-channels-and-underground-spaces-in-the-historic-basin/ |access-date=2026-03-14 |website=Emek Shaveh |language=en}}</ref> In 2019 Elad opened a portion of the road with [[David M. Friedman]], the [[United States Ambassador to Israel]], giving a keynote. According to David M. Halbfinger in ''New York Times'' the ambassador's presence at a public event in East Jerusalem was unusual as ambassadors typically try to "avoid being seen as taking Israel's side in the conflict with the Palestinians".<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Tercatin"/>

[[United States Secretary of State]] [[Marco Rubio]] and United States ambassador to Israel [[Mike Huckabee]] were both present at the inauguration of the site in 2025.  Rubio's visit was criticized by Palestinians and their supporters as endorsing Israeli control and actions in the area.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-16 |title=Marco Rubio inaugurates Israeli settler-led archaeological site |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cg42v2r10kyo |access-date=2026-03-12 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> Ze’ev Orenstein, director of international affairs at the City of David, stated that “All the archeological excavations are carried out by the Israel Antiquities Authority according to the highest standards.”<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lewis |first=Simon |date=2025-09-16 |title=Rubio visits Jerusalem archeological site in boost to Israel's claims |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/rubio-visits-jerusalem-archeological-site-boost-israels-claims-2025-09-15/ |access-date=2026-03-13 |work=Reuters}}</ref>

==Interpretation==
According to archaeologist Ronny Reich, who for several years led the dig uncovering the ancient street together with archaeologist Eli Shukron, pilgrims used the Pool of Siloam as a [[mikveh]] for ritual purification before walking up the street to the [[Second Temple|Temple]].<ref name=Hasson/> However, Yoel Elitzur opposes this interpretation and argues that the Pool of Siloam was a typical Roman public swimming pool.<ref name=Elitzur>{{cite journal |last= Elitzur |first= Yoel |title= The Siloam Pool — 'Solomon's Pool' — Was a Swimming Pool |journal= Palestine Exploration Quarterly |year= 2008 |volume= 140 |issue= 1 (2008) |pages= 17–25 |doi= 10.1179/003103208x269114 |s2cid= 161774603 |url= https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233496309 |access-date=21 July 2020}}</ref>

In ancient times,{{When |date= August 2024}} in the celebration called [[Simchat Beit HaShoeivah]], water was carried up from the [[Pool of Siloam]] to the [[Temple in Jerusalem|Temple]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mishnah Sukkah 4:10 |website= sefaria.org |url=https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Sukkah.4.10?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en}} For Mishnah Sukkah article see [[Moed]].</ref>{{dubious |Who says that this particular street built in 30 CE is ''the'' one used in the festival? When (in what historical period) was this festival celebrated? Who connects the two? Source? Primary sources not accepted. |date= August 2024}} There are attempts to connect the Roman-period street to this festival.

The '''Sheep Gate''' is a [[City gate|town gate]] in [[Trim, County Meath|Trim]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. It is a [[National Monument (Ireland)|National Monument]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.geograph.ie/photo/2696393|title=Geograph:: Trim Town Wall: Sheep Gate (C) Anthony Foster|website=Geograph.ie}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Wakeman Trim Yellow Steeple and Sheep Gate.png|thumb|Illustration from ''Wakeman's handbook of Irish antiquities'' (1903), showing Sheep Gate and [[Yellow Steeple]].]]
The Sheep Gate is the only surviving gate of five that once provided access to Trim. The [[Defensive wall|town wall]] and its gates were built in the 13th or 14th century. Sheep Gate may have been so named as a toll was charged here for [[sheep]] being brought in to be sold at market: in 1290, the [[murage]] and [[pavage]] tax was [[Penny (English coin)|one penny]] per ten sheep, reduced to a [[Farthing (English coin)|farthing]] in 1308. The name could also derive from the archaic meaning of [[wikt:cheap|cheap]], meaning "market" (cf. [[Cheapside]]). This name is not recorded before the 19th century; it may have been known as the Porch Gate, possibly from French ''porte'' ("door"), which may also give its name to the [[Porch Fields]] lying outside the city walls.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://eprints.maynoothuniversity.ie/5121/2/Michael_Potterton_20140624130008.pdf|format=PDF|title=THE ARCHAEOLOGY AND HISTORY OF MEDIEVAL TRIM, COUNTY MEATH|author=Michael Potterton|website=Eprints.maynoothuniversity.ie|access-date=4 November 2021}}</ref> The gate was locked between 9 p.m. and 4 a.m.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lonelyplanet.com/ireland/county-meath/trim/sights/landmarks-monuments/sheep-gate|title=Sheep Gate |website=Lonelyplanet.com}}</ref>

==The gate==
[[File:Trim - Sheep Gate and Castle.jpg|thumb|Sheep Gate with [[Trim Castle]] behind.]]
[[File:Sheeps Gate and Yellow Steeple at Trim Castle.jpg|thumb|left|Sheep Gate with Yellow Steeple behind.]]
[[File:Trim Castle - County Meath (3138577981).jpg|thumb|View of Sheep Gate, with Boyne in foreground.]]
The gate was the southeastern entrance to the town, and is located just north of the [[River Boyne]]. Sheep Gate survives as a stone archway.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irishstones.org/place.aspx?p=403|title=Sheep Gate|website=Irishstones.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.trekearth.com/gallery/Europe/Ireland/North/Meath/photo1393186.htm|title=Ireland|website=Trekearth.com}}</ref>
